summary: Teaches adding and subtracting same-denominator fractions where the result can pass one whole (e.g. 3/5 + 4/5 = 7/5 = 1 2/5). Extends the counting-like-units idea by one step: when the combined count passes the denominator, the extra unit fractions re-group into a whole. Core aims are making children comfortable that a fraction can legitimately exceed one, and fluent at re-unitising an improper result into a mixed number. Addresses the add-across error (3/5 + 4/5 = 7/10), the belief that fractions cannot exceed one, and miscounting the re-group when converting. Covers subtraction too, both within one whole and crossing it from a mixed/improper start.
misconceptions: Adds the denominators as well: 3/5 + 4/5 = 7/10 (add-across; on harder items this error spreads into middle-achieving pupils, NFER).
Believes a fraction cannot exceed one whole, so forces the result — stops at 5/5 = 1, or flips 7/5 to 5/7 — rather than accepting an improper fraction.
Miscounts the re-grouping when converting improper to mixed (e.g. 7/5 = 2 2/5 or 1 3/5), losing track of how many wholes the denominator makes.

activities.title: Spilling into the next whole: an adding model across two bars
steps: Set up two identical bars side by side, each partitioned into the SAME fixed unit (e.g. eighths), with the denominator kept locked so only the count of pieces changes.
Add 7/8 + 3/8 by placing eighth-pieces: fill the first bar with eight eighths, then let the remaining two eighths land in the second bar.
When a full set of denominator-many pieces (eight eighths) completes the first bar, group that full set into a single 'one whole' tile, so the child watches the whole form from the count.
Read the quantity both ways on the same shaded amount: as an improper fraction 10/8 and as a mixed number 1 2/8.
Repeat with 3/5 + 4/5: count fifths past 5/5 and re-group 7/5 as 1 2/5.

Do subtraction too: a within-whole case (5/6 − 2/6 = 3/6) where like units are simply separated, and a genuine crossing-the-whole case from a mixed/improper start that requires re-grouping a whole back into unit fractions (e.g. 1 1/5 − 3/5 = 6/5 − 3/5 = 3/5), treating both as separating like units.
activities.insight: A fraction can exceed one whole; when the running count of unit fractions reaches the denominator those pieces re-group into one whole, which is how an improper fraction becomes a mixed number — seen, not memorised. Subtraction reverses the same re-grouping when a whole must be broken back into unit fractions.

activities.title: Counting on past one whole on a number line
steps: Mark a number line from 0 extending past 1, with tick marks at each unit fraction (fifths past 5/5).
Place 3/5, then count on four more fifth-steps (4/5 in total), landing at 7/5 and noting where the count crossed the 1 mark.
State how many unit steps are before 1 and how many are after, reading off the mixed number 1 2/5.
Repeat for 7/8 + 3/8, identifying the point where the total passes one whole.
activities.insight: Adding same-denominator fractions is counting on in the unit fraction; passing the '1' mark shows concretely that the result is more than one whole and where the mixed-number remainder comes from.

activities.title: Check and explain: improper and mixed forms
steps: Work out 3/5 + 4/5 and 7/8 + 3/8, writing each answer first as an improper fraction and then as a mixed number, showing each step.
Match improper fractions to their mixed-number equivalents on the same shaded quantity (e.g. 10/8 ↔ 1 2/8).
Explain in words why the denominator stays fixed while the count grows.
Respond to a friend's claim that 7/8 + 3/8 = 10/16: simplify 10/16, compare its size with 7/8, and judge whether adding could make the total smaller.
activities.insight: Requiring both the improper and mixed form, plus a magnitude check, reveals whether the child can re-group the whole or is only manipulating symbols; adding two positive same-denominator fractions cannot shrink the total below either addend.

checkQuestion: Work these out, showing each step: 3/5 + 4/5, and 7/8 + 3/8. Write each answer as an improper fraction and then as a mixed number.
checkAnswer: 3/5 + 4/5 = 7/5 = 1 2/5. 7/8 + 3/8 = 10/8 = 1 2/8 (= 1 1/4 simplified). Denominator stays fixed; add the counts; re-group the whole.
